 The craze for weight-loss pills poses many risks.
 VTV.vn - The craze for weight-loss drugs is fueling a surge in the illegal drug market in Brazil and a boom in dietary supplements in the US, posing numerous risks to consumers.
 Đài truyền hình Việt Nam • 23/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 Rapid weight-loss drugs are creating a global craze, fueling a multi-billion dollar market. However, alongside medical advances comes a rise in smuggled drugs and related supplements. From Brazil to the United States, regulatory agencies are grappling with the challenge of balancing access to treatment with user safety.
 In Brazil, customs officials have discovered weight-loss pills hidden in jam jars, motorcycle exhaust pipes, and even under shoe soles at the border with Paraguay. High demand and the continued high price of genuine weight-loss drugs are fueling the smuggled weight-loss drug market in this South American country.
 Taiane Torres, a user of weight-loss medication, said that although she knew the drug she was using was not permitted in Brazil, she decided to try it because she wanted to lose weight and managed to lose 4 kg in a month.
 According to investment bank Itaú BBA, the Brazilian weight-loss drug market could reach $7 billion this year. Approximately 51% of sales are expected to come from prescription drugs and smuggled products. Smuggled drugs, in particular, do not undergo Brazil's official evaluation and control processes.
 Wellington Vieira, a police inspector, said there are groups operating in this underground market, linking with medical clinics, beauty salons, and individual sellers to conduct illegal transactions. The risks lie not only in the origin of the drugs but also in how they are used. 
 Vitoria Leal, a woman in Rio de Janeiro, increased her weight-loss medication dosage without consulting a doctor. She reported that after increasing the dose to 5 mg, she suffered from headaches for a week, completely lost her appetite, and felt nauseous at the sight of food. 
 (Screenshot)
 Between 2018 and mid-August 2026, Brazil recorded more than 3,600 reports of complications and 83 deaths under investigation linked to weight-loss drugs. Authorities have not yet determined the role of smuggled drugs in these cases.
 You may also like Forensic expert Flavio Fabres argues that the use of medication should be medically supervised, with doctors determining the appropriate dosage for each patient.
 Brazil is stepping up its crackdown on smuggling while simultaneously approving more affordable, legalized medications. However, with the demand for rapid weight loss products remaining high, controlling supply and raising consumer awareness continue to be challenges for health authorities.
 Drugs of unknown origin are only part of the story. In the U.S., even those using legal weight-loss medications are becoming customers of another market: dietary supplements.
 After using GLP-1 weight-loss medication, Allison Vecchio, a 42-year-old nurse in Florida, experienced fatigue, weakness, and side effects that affected her daily life. She began looking for fiber, collagen, and electrolyte supplements, costing between $200 and $300 per month. 
 Allison said that when her doctor reduced the dosage of her medication to a level her body could tolerate, she began researching additional supplements to improve effectiveness and achieve the desired results, but it took quite a while to find the right balance.
 Allison's story reflects a rapidly growing consumer trend in the U.S. According to a survey by the Nutrition Business Journal, nearly half of people taking GLP-1 medication begin taking additional vitamins or supplements after treatment. 
 (Screenshot)
 Sales of dietary supplements in the US exceeded $74 billion in 2025. Protein, fiber, and collagen products were particularly popular. Social media also became a crucial advertising and sales channel, with dietary supplement sales on TikTok Shop in the US surpassing $1 billion last year.
 You may also like However, doctors warn that not all products advertised as supporting GLP-1 users have sufficient scientific evidence. In the US, dietary supplements generally do not go through the same pre-sale approval process as prescription drugs.
 Associate Professor Jonathan Bonnet of Stanford University stated that the worrying aspect is that the supplement market is not as tightly regulated as the pharmaceutical market. Buyers may not know exactly what ingredients they are using or whether the product contains harmful substances.
 US regulators are considering tightening regulations on the ingredients and marketing of dietary supplements. Experts suggest that supplements should only be considered when diet and lifestyle don't adequately meet nutritional needs, and only with professional advice.
 From the risk of counterfeit and smuggled goods to the dangers of an unregulated supplement market, the trend of rapid weight loss is posing numerous challenges to healthcare management. Weight loss is a long-term journey, and medical or nutritional interventions only truly provide value when closely monitored by experts, because the ultimate goal remains a healthy and safe body.
